summary: Something your plans rely on that you expect to be true but have not proved.
example: Produce that fails a check at the depot can be sorted, repacked or cooled the same day instead of thrown away. The Quality Check Rollout relies on this.
definition: Something that has to be true for one step of your plan to lead to the next, which you have not proved. You name it on the step that depends on it: a step in a programme's pathway, or a project's success criterion. If it turns out false, you change the plan. It is not a risk (something that might go wrong, which you reduce), not a fixed limit on the work, and not something the work waits on.

cues.assumption: something you expect to be true but have not proved

/metadata/name.guide: A short title that names the condition in a few words.
good: Depots release staff for training during the season
A fault found at intake can still be put right

poor.why: Names a topic, not what has to be true.

/spec/statement.guide: What has to be true, in one sentence about the world, not about your own work.
good: Depots let checkers off the floor for a training day while produce is still coming in.
Produce failing a check at intake can be sorted, repacked or cooled on the same day rather than written off.
Retail buyers price a supplier on how consistent its deliveries are, not only on the best of them.

poor.text: We will arrange cover for checkers on training days.
poor.why: A plan for the work, not a condition in the world. Say what has to be true (depots release staff), not what the team will do.

poor.text: The scanners might break during the pilot.
poor.why: Something that might go wrong is a risk. Add it to the project's risks instead.
This is the result you want, not a condition. Say what has to be true for the training to work.

poor.text: Depots release staff and buyers pay more for consistent produce.
poor.why: Two assumptions in one sentence. Write each one separately.

/spec/ifFalse.guide: Which step stops working if this is not true, and what that does to the result you want.
good: Training waits for the closed season, so the shared standard arrives a season after the produce it was meant to grade.
Checking earlier finds the same faults sooner and loses the same produce, so the programme moves the paperwork and not the outcome.

poor.why: Too broad to act on; say which step stops working and what that does.
That is a response to a risk. Say what goes wrong in the plan if this is false.

/spec/confidence.guide: How sure you are that it is true: high, medium or low. Say why in the note.

/spec/testedBy.guide: How you would find out if it is true: a KPI that would change, or a data source you could check. Leave it empty if there is none, and say so in the note.

poor.why: Not a source you can check. Name the KPI or data source that would show it.

/spec/note.guide: Where the assumption came from, and who doubts it and why. Name roles or teams, not people.
good: The two pilot depots agreed; the rest were not asked.
Held by the market access team from two buyer conversations, not from a price schedule.

poor.why: Names a person and says nothing about what was checked. Name the role or team, and what they found.

Programme:/spec/pathway/-/assumes.ask: Which step in a programme's pathway depends on this being true?
Programme:/spec/pathway/-/assumes.ifNone: Add the step to the programme's pathway first, then name this assumption on it.

Project:/spec/successCriteria/-/assumes.ask: Which success criterion of a project depends on this being true?
Project:/spec/successCriteria/-/assumes.ifNone: Add the success criterion to the project first, then name this assumption on it.
